clinicalPearls: Axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy caused by mutations in GDAP1, the gene for ganglioside-induced differentiation-associated protein 1, a protein of the outer mitochondrial membrane involved in mitochondrial fission.
GDAP1 mutations can be inherited in both patterns: dominant CMT2K is generally milder and later in onset, whereas recessive GDAP1 disease is early and severe.
The gene is markedly pleiotropic, also underlying recessive demyelinating CMT4A and intermediate phenotypes, so GDAP1 disease spans axonal, demyelinating and intermediate forms.
Vocal cord paresis (hoarse or weak voice, stridor) and diaphragmatic or respiratory weakness are characteristic, particularly in the recessive form.
Recessive cases often show early foot and hand deformity, marked distal wasting and loss of ambulation in adolescence or early adult life.
Nerve conduction studies typically reveal reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes with variable, sometimes intermediate, conduction velocities.
Because GDAP1 regulates mitochondrial dynamics, the axons with the greatest energy and transport demands degenerate first.
Determining whether inheritance is dominant or recessive is essential for accurate recurrence-risk counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2K is caused by mutations in GDAP1 (chromosome 8), which encodes ganglioside-induced differentiation-associated protein 1, an anchored protein of the outer mitochondrial membrane expressed in neurons and Schwann cells. GDAP1 promotes mitochondrial fission and regulates the mitochondrial network, mitochondrial movement along axons and interactions between mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum, thereby supporting calcium homeostasis and local energy supply. Dominant (heterozygous) mutations, which produce the milder CMT2K phenotype, typically impair fission through a dominant-negative or haploinsufficient effect, whereas biallelic recessive mutations cause a more severe, earlier disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and can yield axonal, demyelinating (CMT4A) or intermediate neuropathy depending on the specific variants. Impaired mitochondrial trafficking and bioenergetic failure preferentially affect the longest, most metabolically demanding motor and sensory axons, and involvement of the phrenic and laryngeal nerves accounts for the characteristic diaphragmatic and vocal cord weakness.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4A (GDAP1), the recessive demyelinating counterpart of the same gene
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2H (GDAP1) and other GDAP1-related phenotypes
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (MFN2), another mitochondrial-dynamics axonal neuropathy
Other early-onset severe recessive axonal neuropathies
Neuropathies associated with vocal cord and diaphragm involvement of alternative genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise the axonal (or intermediate) pattern and severity
GDAP1 sequencing with analysis of both alleles to distinguish dominant from recessive disease
Laryngoscopy to detect vocal cord paresis
Respiratory function assessment for diaphragmatic weakness
Detailed pedigree and enquiry into consanguinity to clarify inheritance pattern
Nerve biopsy in selected cases, which may show axonal loss with or without demyelinating features reflecting the GDAP1 spectrum
redFlags: Hoarseness, stridor or vocal cord paresis indicating laryngeal nerve involvement
Breathlessness, orthopnoea or nocturnal hypoventilation suggesting diaphragmatic weakness
Rapidly progressive weakness in childhood with early loss of ambulation, typical of severe recessive disease
Respiratory decompensation, which can be life-threatening and warrants urgent assessment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends strongly on inheritance: recessive GDAP1 disease is often severe with early onset, marked disability and potential respiratory compromise, whereas dominant CMT2K tends to be later-onset and milder with preserved ambulation. Respiratory and vocal cord involvement are the principal determinants of morbidity in severe cases.
pitfalls: Overlooking vocal cord and respiratory involvement can delay recognition of serious, potentially treatable complications.
Assuming a single inheritance pattern is a common error, as GDAP1 causes both dominant and recessive disease with very different recurrence risks.
The broad GDAP1 phenotypic spectrum means conduction velocity alone cannot reliably classify the neuropathy as purely axonal.
In consanguineous families a mild dominant carrier may be misread as unaffected, obscuring the true genetic pattern.
references: Peripheral and hereditary neuropathy reference texts
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care via a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Respiratory surveillance with sitting and supine pulmonary function testing and non-invasive ventilation for diaphragmatic weakness
Laryngological assessment of vocal cord paresis with airway monitoring and protection
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for distal weakness and hand and foot deformity
Orthopaedic review for foot deformity and scoliosis
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Genetic counselling clarifying dominant versus recessive inheritance, with family screening
